verdict_reasoning: The goal has lasting demand and nothing survived at levels 1a or 1b. At level 2, v2 does not say how a client or server turns compression on or off (standards-compat-1), which is the kind of question that blocked [P5]. The default also decides the TLS length-leak exposure (security-1) and the replication use case (replication-ondisk-1). These points are fixable, but the list needs to agree on them before code review is useful.

brief.title: Wire protocol compression with a CompressedMessages message, zstd first
brief.problem: Query results and WAL streams travel uncompressed between server and client, which costs network bandwidth. The thread names no specific user group, but the author expects replication to benefit through primary_conninfo. Four earlier attempts did not land.
brief.proposed_design: The server wraps backend messages in a new CompressedMessages message. A compression layer stacks on top of PQcommMethods and uses streaming compression, and libpq decompresses through a new msg_buffer. The client lists its codecs in the _pq_.supported_compressions startup option. In v2, Borodin narrows this to zstd negotiated at startup, compressing only DataRow and CopyData, with frames that end at every ReadyForQuery.
user_visible_surface: New protocol message CompressedMessages; v1 carries the algorithm and a list of nested message types, v2 compresses only DataRow and CopyData.
New startup option _pq_.supported_compressions sent by libpq; v1 claims no protocol version bump is needed.
v1 GUCs protocol_backend_compression, _allowed_algorithms, _threshold, _number_messages and _transaction_frame; v2 drops the public tuning knobs.
New libpq connection parameters trace_file and trace_flags, plus PQTRACE and PQTRACEFLAGS environment variables (from a bundled patch set).
v2 adds client-to-server COPY compression; protocol tracing marks nested messages with "B*".
author_claims: A pgbouncer-style pooler can forward compressed messages without decompressing them, because the messages a pooler inspects stay uncompressed.
Streaming caps backend memory at about 1.3 MB of compression context plus a 131 KB output buffer.
With batches of 2000 or more messages, zstd shrinks a full pgbench_accounts scan from 1 GB to 18 MB at about uncompressed latency.
v1 default batching raises select_all latency from 55 ms to 70 ms; v2 cuts first-row latency from 13 ms to about 0.5 ms.
WAL streaming can be compressed by setting options in primary_conninfo.
brief.thread_state: Andrey Borodin, author of an earlier attempt, proposed merging the two efforts, and Bonnefoy agreed to most of the scope cuts. Borodin posted a reduced v2 on 2026-10-23 and asked whether it works as a common base, and nobody has answered yet.
unclear: No documentation is written yet, and the CF entry is tagged Missing Docs.
The thread does not say whether the protocol needs a minor version bump instead of a _pq_ option, and the author is unsure himself.
The thread does not address CRIME/BREACH-style attacks when compression is used with TLS.
The thread does not say how v2 turns compression on, or whether the server can refuse or limit it.
Nobody has measured the server CPU cost of compression.
v1 bundles the separate PQTRACE patch set; the thread does not say whether it is a prerequisite for v2 tests.

objections.title: v2 does not define how users or servers turn compression on or off
objections.failure_scenario: A site upgrades libpq and the server, and existing applications and standbys start sending zstd-compressed DataRow and CopyData without anyone asking for it. The DBA wants it off for TLS connections or CPU-bound hosts and finds no server setting for that. If instead the default is off, the primary_conninfo recipe from message #1 no longer works.
objections.argument: v2 (message #7) negotiates zstd at startup and drops every public GUC, but it does not say whether libpq advertises zstd by default, which connection parameter controls it, or how the server refuses. In v1, protocol_backend_compression_allowed_algorithms='none' gave the server a veto, and v2 removes it without a replacement. The replication claim in message #1 rests on a GUC that v2 removed. In [P5], unclear compression UI was called a blocker.
objections.author_must_show: What is the default for a libpq client and a server after upgrade, and which parameter lets a client opt out and a server refuse?

critic.reasoning: Message #7 says only that v2 negotiates Zstandard at startup, and it drops the v1 veto protocol_backend_compression_allowed_algorithms='none' without naming a replacement. [P5] stalled on unclear compression UI, so the precedent applies.

objections.title: Compression under TLS reopens CRIME-style leaks with no server-side default off
objections.failure_scenario: An application returns rows that mix a secret column with a column an attacker can write, such as a comment field. Both rows land in one zstd frame that runs until ReadyForQuery. An attacker who can watch TLS record sizes changes the input and reads the secret from the compressed length, and nobody notices.
objections.argument: Postgres disabled SSL compression because of this class of attack. The v2 frame covers every DataRow before ReadyForQuery, so attacker data and secret data share one compression context. The thread does not mention the attack, does not say how v2 turns compression on, and does not say whether the server can refuse it. Review of [P3] asked for the server setting to default to off for security reasons, which applies here.
objections.author_must_show: Is compression off unless the server administrator enables it, and how do the docs tell users when mixing secret and attacker-controlled data under TLS is unsafe?

critic.reasoning: The backend disables SSL compression for this class of attack, and a v2 frame holds every DataRow up to ReadyForQuery. The thread does not mention the attack or state a default, and the [P3] review asked for default off.

objections.title: Frame and flush rules do not cover COPY BOTH replication streams
objections.failure_scenario: A standby streams WAL through a compressed connection. The walsender treats WAL as sent while part of it still sits in the compression context, and the primary shuts down for a switchover. The standby lacks the last WAL, or a synchronous commit waits on a standby reply held in libpq's compression buffer until wal_sender_timeout.
objections.argument: v2 closes backend frames at ReadyForQuery and frontend frames at CopyDone/CopyFail (message #7). A START_REPLICATION session sends neither for its whole life, so only flush behaviour applies. The walsender uses non-blocking sends and pq_is_send_pending() to decide it has caught up and may exit, and the proposal does not say that a buffered 32 KiB input counts as pending. Message #1 offers replication as a main use, so this path needs a stated invariant.
objections.author_must_show: How does v2 guarantee that every pq_flush, pq_flush_if_writable and PQflush pushes all buffered input to the peer during START_REPLICATION, including walsender shutdown and standby replies?

critic.reasoning: Message #7 says existing flush points still apply, but a START_REPLICATION stream never reaches ReadyForQuery. The thread does not say whether input held in the compression context counts as pending for pq_is_send_pending(), and this cannot be checked without the code.

objections.title: Startup option without a protocol version bump leaves negotiation rules open
objections.failure_scenario: A new libpq sends _pq_.supported_compressions to an older server or a proxy that does not know it. The client then needs a defined rule for learning that compression is off, and the proposal gives none. Drivers that implement the protocol themselves cannot tell from the protocol version whether CompressedMessages may appear.
objections.argument: Message #1 adds a new backend message type and says it does not think a version bump is needed, but adds "I'm not sure what are the rules here". v2 keeps the startup-option approach and does not return to the question. Recent protocol work moved toward minor version negotiation, so a committer would likely ask the patch to state its choice and how NegotiateProtocolVersion handles the unknown option.
objections.author_must_show: Why is a _pq_ option enough for a new message type, and how does the client learn that the server or proxy declined it?

critic.reasoning: One part is overstated: NegotiateProtocolVersion already lets a server report an unknown _pq_ option. But message #1 says the author is unsure of the rules, and v2 does not say how libpq treats that reply.

objections.title: Client-to-server COPY decompression has no stated memory bound
objections.failure_scenario: A user with only COPY FROM STDIN on a temp table sends zstd frames that declare a very large window or expand at high ratio. Each backend allocates the decompression window and output, and a few connections exhaust server memory. The administrator sees this only when the OOM killer restarts the cluster.
objections.argument: Message #7 adds client-to-server COPY compression, so the server now decompresses data that any authenticated user controls. Message #1 gives a memory cap only for backend compression, not for decompression. The proposal says nothing about a maximum zstd window, a limit on decompressed size per message, or whether the server can turn off inbound compression. libpq has the same exposure when it connects to an untrusted server.
objections.author_must_show: What caps the memory a backend and libpq spend decompressing peer-supplied frames, including the zstd window size, and can the server disable inbound compression?

critic.reasoning: Streaming decompression bounds the output buffer and zstd rejects windows above 128 MiB by default, so the high-ratio part is weak. The window allocation per backend is still peer-controlled, and the thread states no cap or inbound off switch.

other_surviving.title: Server has no control over compression CPU cost in v2
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A newer libpq offers zstd at startup, and every connection from an application fleet starts compressing large result sets. Backend CPU use on a shared server rises, and the operator has no setting to refuse or limit compression. The operator notices this only under load.
other_surviving.argument: v1 had protocol_backend_compression_allowed_algorithms='none' as an off switch (message #1). v2 removes the public knobs and negotiates at startup (message #7), and the thread does not say whether the server can refuse. Nobody has measured server CPU cost. Every user of the server pays this cost, and only clients that request compression gain from it.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How does an administrator turn off or restrict compression in v2, what is the default, and what backend CPU cost does it add per compressed MiB?

critic.reasoning: The off-switch part repeats standards-compat-1, but the CPU point is separate. The benchmarks in message #1 report latency and wire size only, and no message measures backend CPU cost.

refuted.title: v2 does not say how users enable or refuse compression
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA reviewing v2 cannot tell whether compression is turned on by a libpq connection parameter, a server setting, or automatically once both sides support zstd. A reviewer ends up in the same position as the 2024 attempt and cannot judge the interface. Users who upgrade libpq may find compression in use without having asked for it.
refuted.argument: The 2024 attempt [P5] was blocked on user-interface questions, with "these UI questions are blockers" as the key sentence. v1 used five GUCs plus an options string. Message #7 drops the public knobs and says only that v2 "negotiates Zstandard at startup". No message describes the client option, the server-side control, or the defaults that replace the GUCs, so the issue that stopped [P5] is still open.
refuted.author_must_show: What exact client connection parameter and server setting control compression in v2, what are their defaults, and how does a server refuse it?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which covers the same missing enable and refuse controls and also names the removed server veto and the default after upgrade.

refuted.title: Security default and TLS compression risk not addressed
refuted.failure_scenario: An application returns rows that hold both attacker-supplied text and a secret token, over TLS with compression negotiated. An observer who can see ciphertext lengths and repeat the query learns the secret byte by byte. The operator finds out only after a disclosure, because nothing in the setup warned them.
refuted.argument: The [P3] review asked for the server setting to default to off for security reasons. The backend still disables SSL compression for this class of attack. v2 compresses DataRow within a frame that lasts until ReadyForQuery, so attacker-controlled data and secrets can share a compression context. The thread does not discuss CRIME/BREACH-style attacks and does not state the default.
refuted.author_must_show: Is compression off by default on the server in v2, and what is the stated position on length-leak attacks when it is combined with TLS?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of security-1, which states the same length-leak scenario and the same question about a server default of off.

refuted.title: Pooler forwarding assumes client and server negotiated the same codec
refuted.failure_scenario: A transaction pooler opens a server connection with zstd and then assigns it to a client that did not advertise zstd, or that uses an older libpq. The pooler forwards CompressedMessages as the proposal suggests. The client fails to parse the result on its first large query.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says pgbouncer can forward compressed messages "assuming the client supports the compression algorithm". Compression is fixed per server connection at startup in v2, so a pooler must either split pools by client capability or decompress. Neither option is spelled out, and proxies that forward startup packets but parse DataRow are not discussed.
refuted.author_must_show: What must a pooler do when the client's advertised codecs differ from those its server connection negotiated?

critic.reasoning: The scenario needs a pooler that requests zstd on its server connection and then forwards to a client that did not advertise it. The pooler sees both startup packets, and message #1 already states the forwarding condition.

refuted.title: v2 drops the only described way to compress replication
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator upgrades a primary with several standbys, logical subscribers and pg_basebackup jobs. Either all of these streams start using zstd with no server setting to refuse it, or none can, because primary_conninfo has no option left to request compression.
refuted.argument: Message #1 enables WAL compression through options='-cprotocol_backend_compression=zstd' in primary_conninfo. v2 removes that GUC, removes session control, and negotiates zstd at startup (message #7). Neither message says which side decides, whether libpq advertises zstd by default, or whether the server can refuse compression for walsenders. The replication benefit claimed in message #1 depends on that answer.
refuted.author_must_show: In v2, which conninfo parameter or server setting turns compression on or off for a walreceiver, logical subscriber or pg_basebackup, and who gets the final say?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which already notes that the primary_conninfo recipe from message #1 depends on a GUC that v2 removed.

refuted.title: Pooler-visible wire contract has nothing that enforces it
refuted.failure_scenario: A later release adds a backend message type that poolers need to read, or puts state into a message that v2 compresses. A pooler that forwards CompressedMessages without decompressing them then loses track of session state. Pooler maintainers find out from field bugs after the release.
refuted.argument: Pooler compatibility rests on two rules: only DataRow and CopyData are compressed, and frames end at every ReadyForQuery (message #3, message #7). The thread treats these rules as a design choice. It does not record them as a protocol promise or add a check that fails when a future patch breaks them. Every later protocol change would have to respect the rules, and a reviewer could miss that.
refuted.author_must_show: Where will the compressible-message set and the frame reset rule be documented as protocol guarantees, and what test fails if a future patch breaks either rule?

critic.reasoning: The scenario depends on a future patch that adds a message type to the compressed set, and v2 compresses only DataRow and CopyData. The missing documentation is already recorded on the CF entry and is outside levels 1-2.

refuted.title: No committer who knows the protocol code has engaged yet
refuted.failure_scenario: The patch changes the parse path in libpq through the new msg_buffer, and it adds a backend PQcommMethods layer and a new protocol message. If it is committed without a qualified owner, a later decoding bug in libpq or a pooler interaction bug waits on whoever pushed it. Users meet the bug through every libpq-based driver.
refuted.argument: The visible thread has two authors and one short correction (message #2). No committer has commented, and the v2 question in message #7 is unanswered. Earlier attempts stalled after review stopped, so their recorded reasons do not apply to this design directly. Only the ownership risk carries over. The libpq change touches pqParseInput3, getCopyMessageData and pqFunctionCall3, which every client uses.
refuted.author_must_show: Which committer familiar with libpq and the protocol layer has agreed to review v2 and own follow-up fixes after commit?

critic.reasoning: This is a committability note. The rubric says weak committability must not count against the design, and the thread is six weeks old with v2 posted three weeks ago.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: Message #1 offers compression of the WAL stream through primary_conninfo, and CopyData compression covers START_REPLICATION.

touch_points.label: wire protocol
touch_points.reason: The proposal adds the CompressedMessages message and the _pq_.supported_compressions startup option.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: A compression layer stacks on PQcommMethods and changes libpq-be.h and libpq.h, and libpq gains connection parameters.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: v1 adds five protocol_backend_compression GUCs; v2 drops the public ones without naming a replacement control.

touch_points.label: psql UX conventions
touch_points.reason: Patch 0007 adds a HIDE_NOTIFICATIONS parameter to psql for regression tests.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: Compression under TLS allows length-leak attacks, and the server decompresses COPY data sent by any authenticated user.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A new protocol message, a zstd dependency in the protocol path and a pooler-visible contract stay for ever.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The backend putmessage and flush path and the libpq parse path (pqParseInput3, pqGet*) change for every connection.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: After upgrade, what is the default for a libpq client and for a server, and which parameter lets a client opt out and a server refuse compression?
Is compression off unless the server administrator enables it, and what is the stated position on CRIME/BREACH-style length leaks when it runs under TLS?
During START_REPLICATION, does every pq_flush, pq_flush_if_writable and PQflush push all input held in the compression context to the peer, including at walsender shutdown?
Why is a _pq_ option enough for a new message type without a minor version bump, and how does libpq learn that the server or a proxy declined it?
What caps the memory that a backend and libpq spend to decompress frames from the peer, including the zstd window size?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the libpq parse path and the frontend/backend protocol, with a view on TLS interaction and walsender flush behaviour. None has spoken in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a new protocol message and negotiation rule that every driver and pooler must handle, with no end date. The owner also signs for the zstd dependency in the protocol path and any security report about compression under TLS.
committability.author_follow_up: Both authors are active: Bonnefoy agreed to most scope cuts, and Borodin posted v2 on 2026-10-23 and asked for agreement on a common base.

priority.reason: Five attempts since 2018 show lasting demand, and the two authors are converging on a smaller scope. The patch set has 16 parts across libpq, the backend and the protocol, so review is better spent once v2 states its enable and refuse controls and its security default.

provisional_note: Only the first 3 of 7 messages and no code were read, so the v2 negotiation, the flush behaviour during replication and the decompression memory limits could not be checked. The cost on the libpq parse path for connections without compression is also unverified.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

A server setting, libpq_compression, controls the allowed algorithms, and each direction of traffic is compressed independently.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use "protocol options" name instead of "protocol extensions" everywhere
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Heikki Linnakangas, Robert Haas, Jacob Champion, Laurenz Albe, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the term "protocol extensions" with "protocol options" in the docs and in a libpq error message, because "extension" suggests a link to Postgres extensions. No protocol options existed yet, so the author saw this as the time to settle on one name.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers did not agree on a new name. Heikki Linnakangas said "protocol option" suggests GUCs, Robert Haas found "protocol extensions" mildly clearer, Jacob Champion preferred keeping "protocol extension" with a docs note, and Laurenz Albe voted to keep "extension" because "option" already names other things in the docs. Peter Eisentraut rejected the patch for lack of consensus to change.

precedents_retrieved.title: Libpq Compression
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch series adds protocol-level compression to the wire protocol, on top of a new layered IO stream abstraction that replaces secure_read and secure_write. Client and server announce supported algorithms through the `_pq_.libpq_compression` startup option and a `ParameterStatus` message, and each side then compresses in either direction without further negotiation.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch after five months without updates, while waiting for the separate discussion on a protocol message to change GUCs. Robert Haas said the user interface was not clear enough to review, citing `libpq_compression=gzip:compress=off` as confusing. He called these UI questions blockers. A reworked syntax with `client_to_server`/`server_to_client` was being discussed when the entry closed.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert changes for SSL compression in libpq
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert changes for SSL compression in libpq
Reverted commit(s): Switch back sslcompression to be a normal input field in libpq; Add support for more progress reporting in COPY
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This partially reverts 096bbf7 and 9d2d457, undoing the libpq changes as
it could cause breakages in distributions that share one single libpq
version across multiple major versions of Postgres for extensions and
applications linking to that.

Note that the backend is unchanged here, and it still disables SSL
compression while simplifying the underlying catalogs that tracked if
compression was enabled or not for a SSL connection.

Per discussion with Tom Lane and Daniel Gustafsson.

precedents_retrieved.title: Password identifiers, protocol aging and SCRAM protocol
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set moves password storage from pg_authid into a new pg_auth_verifiers catalog, allowing one verifier per protocol per role, with a superuser GUC (password_protocols) and a sanitize function used by pg_upgrade to retire outdated protocols. On top of this it adds refactoring patches and SCRAM-SHA1 authentication as a new password protocol.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas argued that the work should move to the next release cycle: these are large, user-facing changes involving wire protocol changes, and they had received little detailed code-level review. He judged that they could not be completed safely in the three weeks before feature freeze, and he questioned whether there was consensus on the direction, including multiple password verifiers. The author agreed that the SCRAM patch (0009) needed more time than remained, and no committer took it on; Magnus Hagander said he lacked time in this CommitFest. The author marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I don't see how we're going to get all of this into 9.6, and these are big, user-facing changes that I don't think we should rush into under time pressure.

precedents_retrieved.title: Hooks and API to allow loadable wire protocol extensions
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add hooks and an API so a loadable extension, listed in shared_preload_libraries, can make the postmaster listen on extra ports and serve a different wire protocol, such as TDS. Extensions register callbacks for accept, authentication, error reporting and the TCOP loop, and the existing backend libpq code registers itself through the same API.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show the closing decision; the thread goes silent in March 2021 and the entry was returned in October. The last review objection shown is that the patch's abstractions are still tied to the libpq protocol (cancel key, ready-for-query, simple and extended query), so an extension could not implement another vendor's protocol through them. The author replied that TDS needs a full replacement of PostgresMain(), and that code was not yet posted.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think, the way the abstractions are chosen in this patch, it is still very much tied to how the libpq protocol works.

precedents_retrieved.title: libpq compression
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds streaming compression of libpq traffic with zlib or zstd, chosen at build time and enabled by a compression connection option, as a replacement for deprecated SSL compression. A compression layer wraps the socket read and write calls in both backend and frontend and passes tx/rx functions into the compression stream.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers objected to the design: the compression option sent in the startup packet, and the compression stream bypassing secure_read()/pqsecure_read() rather than working as a layer under them, which they found invasive. The author and reviewers did not reach consensus on this layering, and Dmitry Dolgov posted an alternative experimental patch. In the last commitfest the patch had failing tests and no review, and the visible messages do not show a closing statement.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I have not actually looked much at your patch, but I am wondering if it could not be possible to make the whole footprint less invasive which really worries me as now shaped.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
Reverted commit(s): Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server Previously, we skipped a checkpoint if no WAL had been written since last checkpoint, though this does not appear in user documentation. As of now, we skip a checkpoint until we have written at least one enough WAL to switch the next WAL file. This greatly reduces the level of activity and number of WAL messages generated by a very low activity server. This is safe because the purpose of a checkpoint is to act as a starting place for a recovery, in case of crash. This patch maintains minimal WAL volume for replay in case of crash, thus maintaining very low crash recovery time.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 18fb9d8d21a28caddb72c7ffbdd7b96d52ff9724.  Per
discussion, it does not seem like a good idea to allow committed changes to
go un-checkpointed indefinitely, as could happen in a low-traffic server;
that makes us entirely reliant on the WAL stream with no redundancy that
might aid data recovery in case of disk failure.

This re-introduces the original problem of hot-standby setups generating a
small continuing stream of WAL traffic even when idle, but there are other
ways to address that without compromising crash recovery, so we'll revisit
that issue in a future release cycle.

Reverted commit(s): Change default value of default_toast_compression to "lz4", when available
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 7c1849311e49, due to the fact that more than 60% of
the buildfarm members do not have lz4 installed.  As we are in the last
commit fest of the development cycle, and that it could take a couple
of weeks to stabilize things, this change is reverted for now.

This commit will be reworked in a lighter version, as
default_toast_compression's default can be changed to "lz4" without the
switch from --with-lz4 to --without-lz4.  This approach will keep the
buildfarm at bay, and still allow builds to take advantage of LZ4 in
TOAST by default, as long as the code is compiled with LZ4 support.

A harder requirement based on LZ4 should be achievable at some point,
but it is going to require some work from the buildfarm owners first.
Perhaps this part could be revisited at the beginning of the next
development cycle.

roaster_notes.note: Message #1 cites three earlier attempts, and message #2 reports a fourth by Borodin that the author had missed. That fourth attempt is now being merged into v2.
Three fixable objections. The bundled PQTRACE parameters are left out because v2 uses the existing libpq testclient instead.
There is no on-disk, WAL record or catalog change. The concerns are limited to the wire protocol as used by replication connections.

Two security objections are raised. Startup and authentication stay uncompressed per message #1, so pre-auth exposure appears unchanged. That is a provisional reading, since v2 negotiation is not described.
The objections above are fixable and do not reject the idea. Hot-path cost for clients that do not use compression could not be checked without the code.

Core has no way to compress protocol traffic since SSL compression was disabled ([P6]). wal_compression, pg_basebackup compression and pg_receivewal --compress do not cover query results or the streaming replication link. An SSH or VPN tunnel with compression works per link, but it cannot cover many application connections or pooled traffic, and the v1 design reuses the existing compression option syntax instead of adding a second one.

Demand has lasted: five attempts by at least five independent authors since 2018 ([P10], [P1], [P3], [P5], message #2), and the removal of SSL compression left no built-in alternative. The thread still lacks a field report with numbers, and the primary_conninfo replication benefit in message #1 has not been measured.
